Its biggest strengths are that useful battery capacity, sensible socket layout and an app that makes the controls understandable. The output ceiling needs consideration, but for compatible equipment, DIY jobs and household backup, there’s plenty to like.

 Portable power stations are useful for everything from keeping your broadband running during a power cut to powering equipment away from a convenient socket. The Anker Solix S2000 fits both roles, combining a substantial battery with a relatively compact upright design.
 What impressed me most, though, was how little fuss it involved. It handled repeated sessions with a 1,200W wet/dry vacuum straight out of the box, while the accompanying app was easy to set up and refreshingly clear about what its settings actually do.

 Design and connections 
 The S2000 has an understated appearance: a dark grey enclosure, rounded edges and a glossy front panel. It looks perfectly at home beside a desk, although mine was soon earning its keep around DIY equipment.
 Its upright shape gives it a reasonably small footprint. At 16.2kg, however, “portable” still involves a deliberate lift. Moving it between rooms or taking it out to the garden is one thing; carrying it a long distance is another.
 The UK version has four proper Type G sockets, split evenly between the front and rear. That arrangement makes sense. You can keep regularly connected equipment plugged in behind the unit, leaving the front sockets available for things you connect occasionally.
 There is a trade-off: you’ll need access to both sides if you want to use every socket. Bear that in mind before squeezing it into a tight space, and leave the ventilation clear.

 The USB connections sit above the display. The 100W USB-C port is the one to choose for a compatible laptop, while the other USB-C connection is limited to 15W. They look similar, so it’s worth checking the labels.
 The screen puts the remaining battery percentage front and centre, alongside input and output wattage and an estimated remaining time. That gives you the information you need without reaching for your phone.
 Performance: a proper day’s work 
 My S2000 arrived with a 59% state of charge. Rather than charging it fully before doing anything useful, I put it straight to work powering a 1,200W wet/dry vacuum.
 Between approximately 10am and 5pm, I used the vacuum repeatedly in sessions lasting around five to ten minutes. The Anker handled those sessions without any problems, and by the time I finished, it still showed 13% remaining.
 To be clear, that was intermittent use across a seven-hour working day, rather than seven hours of continuous vacuuming. Even so, it was a useful practical test: repeated use of a fairly demanding appliance, starting with little more than half a battery.
 The benefit was simple. I could get on with the job without running an extension lead back to a mains socket, and the power station had enough charge to cover the work I needed to do.
 This wasn’t a controlled capacity test. I didn’t record the vacuum’s total running time or measure the energy delivered at the socket, so it wouldn’t be fair to calculate an efficiency figure from the percentage drop.
 What I can say is that it coped comfortably with this particular vacuum and pattern of use.
 The main limitation is the 1,500W continuous output. Battery capacity tells you how much energy is stored; output determines which appliances it can run. A large battery doesn’t automatically mean it can power a typical high-wattage UK kettle or several demanding tools together.
 Check appliance ratings, allow for starting demands, and remember that the output limit is shared across the AC sockets.
 Charging options 
 (Image credit: Future) For everyday charging, the S2000 connects directly to the mains using the supplied AC cable. There’s no separate external power brick to find space for.
 During one charging session, the front display showed approximately 1,068W going in. An app screenshot taken during charging showed around 1,077W, with UltraFast charging switched off. These are snapshots rather than a timed charging test, but they show a substantial charging rate in normal use.
 There’s also an app-controlled UltraFast option when a quicker turnaround matters.
 Away from home, the S2000 supports compatible solar panels and vehicle charging, provided you have the correct cables and accessories. Solar input is capped at 400W, with Anker specifying a maximum open-circuit voltage of 60V. Panel compatibility matters as well as the connector.
 Those alternatives add flexibility, although a normal car accessory socket will be much slower than mains charging. Think of it as a way to replenish charge while travelling, rather than expecting a quick refill of a 2kWh battery.
 The app: easy to set up, easy to understand 
 (Image credit: Future || Anker) The app was one of the nicest surprises.
 Finding it in the Google Play Store was straightforward, as were signing in and getting started. The S2000 was detected straight away, added without difficulty and ready to control. An iPhone version also appears to be available, although my experience here was with Android.
 The main screen presents the battery percentage, temperature, charging estimate and power flow clearly. You can see what’s happening at a glance.
 More useful still is the depth of control. There are multiple UPS and power-management modes, charging timers, adjustable AC charging power and battery charge limits. You also get AC output scheduling, a countdown to switch the sockets off, screen controls and power-usage history.
 Crucially, the explanations are good. Rather than leaving you to decipher a vaguely named mode, the app helps you understand what a setting does and decide whether it suits your needs.
 Some power-station apps make configuration feel like educated guesswork. Here, the guidance makes the extra features more approachable, particularly if this is your first battery system.
 Backup power and everyday use 
 The UPS function adds another potential role: keeping suitable equipment powered when the mains fails. Anker quotes a transfer time of around 10ms, although I haven’t independently measured that or tested compatibility with individual computers.
 For a home office, the combination of rear sockets, battery monitoring and configurable operating modes is appealing. You can leave equipment connected and manage the unit without constantly handling it.

 EcoFlow has been a consistent top-performer in our tests, with one model earning the top spot in our guide to portable power stations. High-capacity, durable build, and reliable output are all strong with this line.
 So, the EcoFlow Delta 3 Classic with 45W solar panel for $479 (was $598) at Best Buy is an easy recommendation. If a power outage leaves you without heat controls, internet, or a working fridge, the Delta 3 Classic gives you a quiet, fume-free backup you can keep indoors.
 • Best for: Professionals, campers, and RV owners who want dependable backup power for outages or portable power on the go.
 • Why we like it: Beyond the strong performance in our tests, this EcoFlow model features 1,024Wh of long-life LFP battery capacity, 1,800W of continuous AC output to run big appliances, 3,000 charge cycles, and a five-year warranty. The solar panels for off-grid use sweeten this one considerably for us.
 • What you need to know: At $479 it’s good value for the battery alone, though the small panel is more of a bonus for added energy security rather than a serious charging option.
 Save $119

This bundle includes a 45W solar panel and a protective bag, and it comes with a five-year warranty. EcoFlow sells and ships it through Best Buy’s marketplace.

 Why We Recommend It
 EcoFlow is one of the biggest names in portable power, and the Delta 3 Classic is a pared-back version of its Delta 3 that keeps the essentials: a large, long-lasting LFP battery and enough output to run a full-size fridge or a space heater for a while. We haven’t tested this model ourselves, so this pick rests on EcoFlow’s track record and our experience testing other models. Expect fast charging, easy of use, and total dependability if you need additional or on-the-move power supply. The five-year warranty adds welcome peace of mind for a product you may rely on in an emergency.
 For more top picks, see our guide to the best portable power stations . 
 Price Context & Historical Value
 This is $119, or 20%, off the bundle’s $598 list price, which is a solid discount on a 1kWh power station with a five-year warranty. Keep in mind that the included 45W panel would take more than a full day of ideal sunlight to refill the battery, so think of it as a top-up tool rather than a full-blown charging solution. If you want backup power in place before winter, this is a good time to buy.
 Should you buy it?

 ❌ Skip the EcoFlow Delta 3 Classic bundle if... you plan to rely on solar charging, since a 45W panel is far too small to refill this battery quickly, you need a power station that’s easy to carry long distances at 26.7 pounds, or you’d prefer to buy directly from Best Buy rather than a marketplace seller.

 What you need to know
 Peak Design has introduced what it calls the world's first Qi2.3-certified magnetic power bank with a built-in kickstand.
 The 5,000mAh power bank supports 15W wireless charging on battery and up to 25W when connected to external power.
 Peak Design's new accessories start at $65, with a lifetime guarantee and additional battery performance coverage.
 Peak Design today introduced a new Qi2.3 magnetic power bank alongside several other charging accessories that put some of the first-party accessories from brands like Samsung and Google to shame.
 Peak Design , the brand popularly known for its backpacks and everyday carry gear, has slowly been expanding into mobile accessories as well. And today, the company unveiled its latest lineup of charging accessories, bringing some pretty interesting features that go beyond what first-party brands like Google and Samsung currently offer.
 One of the most interesting products announced today is the Kickstand Travel Battery, which Peak Design says is the world's first Qi2.3-certified wireless power bank. It packs a 5,000mAh battery and supports up to 25W wireless charging.
 (Image credit: Peak Design) The magnetic power bank delivers up to 15W wireless charging when running on its internal battery, but that increases to 25W when you plug it into a power source. It also features a built-in kickstand, making it easier to prop up your phone while charging.
 The Kickstand Travel Battery starts at $99.95 and comes in two colors, Moon and Black. It's already available to purchase.

 Peak Design is best known for its excellent travel backpacks , camera accessories and cleverly designed everyday carry gear, but the San Francisco-based brand is now turning its attention to charging accessories.
 The company has unveiled a collection of four premium charging essentials, including a magnetic power bank , a foldable wireless charging station, a slimline wall charger and a range of USB-C cables.
 It's a bold move into a category dominated by Anker and Belkin, though Peak Design isn't necessarily trying to compete on price.
 Latest Videos From T3 
 Watch full video here: 
 Instead, the brand is applying the same design philosophy that made its bags and camera accessories popular to everyday gadgets.
 Charging accessories with a Peak Design twist
 For instance, the Wireless Kickstand Travel Battery is a remarkably slim 5,000mAh magnetic power bank measuring only 10.5mm thick.
 You may like

 This power bank has a feature I didn't know I needed, but can't live without now 
 I might have just found the perfect power bank – for a reason I didn't expect 
 Peak Design claims it's the world's first Qi2.3-certified wireless charger that delivers up to 15W of wireless power on its internal battery, increasing to 25W when connected to an external power source.
 (Image credit: Peak Design)
 Its integrated aluminium kickstand makes it especially appealing for travel and lets you prop up your phone in portrait or landscape.
 Sign up to the T3 newsletter for smarter living straight to your inbox
 Get all the latest news, reviews, deals and buying guides on gorgeous tech, home and active products from the T3 experts
 It also supports pass-through charging, so you can top up the battery and your phone at the same time.
 The Wireless Charging Station 2-in-1 might be an even better option for people who travel with multiple devices, featuring two equally capable Qi2.2 magnetic charging pads, each delivering up to 25W.
 (Image credit: Peak Design)
 This setup lets you charge two compatible phones at once, while an additional USB-C port powers a third device, such as a smartwatch.
 What to read next
 I have a new favourite charging stand for my iPhone – its simplicity is why it wins 
 Twelve South's new charging tray is a slice of luxury – which doesn't mean you need it, per se 
 Jackery's new portable power stations are dramatically smaller and lighter, but there's another clever upgrade 
 The aluminium stand features an adjustable hinge for positioning devices at different viewing angles and folds flat when it's time to pack up.
 Small chargers, serious power
 Peak Design has also introduced the Dual Slim Charger, a 65W GaN wall charger that measures just 13mm thick.
 Despite its slender profile, it has two USB-C ports that can charge a laptop and phone simultaneously, automatically sharing power between the connected devices.
 Depending on what's plugged in, the charger can split its output into two 30W feeds or allocate 45W to one device and 20W to the other.
 It also has fold-flat prongs that make it easier to slip into a travel pouch, and sports graphene-based thermal management that is said to help keep temperatures in check.
 (Image credit: Peak Design)
 Lastly, the UltraStrand USB-C cables are available in Everyday and Pro configurations.
 The Everyday version supports up to 60W charging and 480Mbps data transfer speeds, while the Pro cable supports 240W and 40Gbps, respectively.
 Whether Peak Design’s new collection is worth choosing over the considerably broader ranges offered by Anker and Belkin remains to be seen.
 (Image credit: Peak Design)
 However, it's refreshing to see another established accessories brand putting some thought into how everyday charging gadgets look and function.
 The new charging collection is available at Peak Design US from today, 3 November 2026.
 The Wireless Kickstand Travel Battery and Wireless Charging Station 2-in-1 are priced at $99.95 each.
 The Dual Slim Charger costs $64.95, and UltraStrand cables start at $24.95. Global rollout is expected by mid-November.

 General market pricing in 2026: compact 70-190Wh AC models typically sit in the $150 to $280 range, 250-300Wh models in the $220 to $380 range, and 600W-class models like the EB3A often $280 to $420 depending on sales and solar bundles.
 How to choose: continuous watts beats peak watts
 Manufacturers advertise surge watts prominently. Ignore that for buying. What runs your gear is continuous AC output.
 Under 150W continuous: Enough for laptop bricks, phone and camera chargers, LED lights, routers, portable monitors. Best for air travel carry-on size and light packs. Example type: Omni 20+, Yeti 200X.
 300W continuous: The sweet spot for travel and backup. Runs most laptops, Starlink Mini/router setups, mini fans, CPAPs with heated humidifier off, and small TVs for a short time. Example type: River 2, Explorer 300 Plus, Solix C300.
 600W continuous: Adds small kitchen gear, power tools on low, larger monitors, and mini-fridges at startup. Heavier and louder under load. Example type: EB3A.
 Also check inverter type. All models listed above use pure sine wave AC, which is required for sensitive electronics, laptop power supplies, and medical devices. Avoid modified sine wave units for anything except simple resistive loads.
 Worked calculation: how many laptop charges and how long will it run?
 You cannot divide station Wh by laptop Wh directly. AC inversion loses 10-20%, plus the laptop brick loses another 5-10%. Use 0.82 as a realistic efficiency factor for AC charging:
 Usable AC energy = Rated Wh x 0.82
Recharges = Usable AC energy / Laptop battery Wh
Runtime hours = Usable AC energy / Device watts
 Example for a 70Wh thin-and-light laptop and a 60W work load:
 EcoFlow River 2 (256Wh): 256 x 0.82 = 210Wh usable. That is 3.0 full recharges, or about 3.5 hours running a 60W load continuously.
 Bluetti EB3A (268Wh): 268 x 0.82 = 220Wh usable. That is 3.1 recharges, or 3.6 hours at 60W, or about 27 minutes at a full 480W load.
 OmniCharge Omni 20+ (71Wh): 71 x 0.82 = 58Wh usable. That is 0.8 recharges – enough to add 70-80% to most 13-14 inch laptops once, or run a 25W camera charger and mirrorless batteries for about 2.3 hours.
 If you plan to charge via USB-C PD instead of AC, efficiency rises to about 0.90-0.92. A 256Wh station can add 15-20% more laptop runtime over USB-C than over AC. Whenever your laptop supports USB-C charging, use it and save the AC outlet for devices that truly need it.
 Do not forget airline limits
 The Omni 20+ at 71Wh is under the 100Wh FAA/TSA carry-on limit without airline approval. All 187Wh to 288Wh models above exceed carry-on limits for lithium batteries and cannot go on passenger aircraft. They are car, train, and home backup products, not flight products. If you fly frequently, the sub-100Wh class is your only AC option.
 Which one fits your situation?
 Best for travel by car and remote work: EcoFlow River 2
 The River 2 wins for most buyers because it combines 300W of usable AC, very fast 1-hour wall recharge, and LiFePO4 longevity in a 3.5 kg package. It will recharge a MacBook Air/Windows ultrabook 2.5-3 times over AC, or run a router + laptop for 3-4 hours. It also supports pass-through and UPS-style switching under 30ms, useful for keeping a router alive during short outages.
 Limitation: 300W will not start most heating elements, kettles, or full-size power tools.
 Best for home backup and higher loads: Bluetti EB3A
 Choose the EB3A if you need to run a 400-500W device briefly, such as a mini-fridge compressor startup, desktop PC with monitor, or CPAP with humidifier on. The 600W inverter is twice as capable as other models in this weight class, and it retains LiFePO4 chemistry. The tradeoff is weight at 4.6 kg and more fan noise at high load.
 Best lightweight all-rounder: Jackery Explorer 300 Plus and Anker Solix C300
 Both offer around 288Wh and 300W AC with LiFePO4 cells. Pick the Jackery if you want a simpler interface and broad solar panel support for camping. Pick the Anker Solix C300 if you want faster combined USB-C output for charging multiple laptops and phones alongside AC, plus a slightly more compact rectangular form for packing in a car trunk.
 Neither is flight-legal, so choose based on port layout and recharge speed rather than capacity alone.
 Best ultra-portable AC power: OmniCharge Omni 20+
 The Omni 20+ is the only true power-bank-sized option here with a real 100W AC outlet. It fits in a jacket pocket and is flight-legal. It is ideal for photographers who need to charge proprietary camera batteries, drone batteries, or a laptop brick where USB-C is not available. Expect one partial laptop charge, not multiple. The small fan runs during AC use and the unit gets warm, which is normal.
 Best for minimal weight with low-power AC: Goal Zero Yeti 200X
 The Yeti 200X provides 120W AC at only 2.3 kg, lighter than any 300W station. It suits CPAP users without heated humidity, field monitors, and lighting kits. Its older NMC chemistry is rated for about 500 cycles versus 2,000-3,000 for LiFePO4 models, so it is better for occasional use than daily cycling.

 Ownership realities: what wears out and common mistakes
 AC power stations fail differently than USB banks. The battery usually outlasts the inverter fan and ports if you use LiFePO4 models daily.
 Fan and vents clog first. Lint and car dust reduce cooling, forcing louder fan speeds. Vacuum vents monthly and never run AC output inside a closed bag. Overheating triggers throttling from 300W down to 150-200W.
 Do not store at 100%. LiFePO4 tolerates it better than NMC, but for storage over 2 weeks, leave at 50-60% and top up every 3 months. Storing full and hot is the fastest way to lose capacity.
 Avoid tiny loads on AC. Running a 5W phone charger from the AC outlet can waste 8-12W in inverter overhead. Use USB-C for anything under 20W to double runtime.
 Pass-through limits. Charging the station while running AC is convenient, but sustained pass-through at high watts generates heat. For daily desk backup, use the dedicated UPS mode if available and keep loads under 70% of rated watts.
 Cables matter. The included AC cable and wall brick are sized for fast recharge. Using a thin extension cord or underrated car inverter to recharge can double recharge time or trip thermal protection.
 For maintenance, cycle LiFePO4 models from 100% to 0% to 100% once every 3 months to recalibrate the battery meter. If the display shows 30% then suddenly drops to 0% under load, calibration is overdue, not battery failure.
 Final pick by need
 If you want one portable outlet for travel and backup in 2026, get a 256-288Wh LiFePO4 model with 300W AC, such as the EcoFlow River 2 or Anker Solix C300. Step up to the Bluetti EB3A only if you have a specific 400-600W device to run. Choose the OmniCharge Omni 20+ only if you must fly with AC power or carry it on foot all day, and accept one partial laptop charge as the tradeoff.

Port layout is clean: the two USB-C inputs sit side by side, the USB-A ports are below, and the AC outlets are separated, so cables don't crowd each other when you're charging multiple devices.
 The two-way USB-C1 does the heavy lifting here at 65W input and output, which means you can fast-charge a laptop and feed power back into the station simultaneously if you're running AC input at the same time. That dual-input design saves real time on a job site when you need to top up and keep devices running.
 Wall Recharge in 1.3 Hours, Solar in 2.2 Hours
 From a standard wall outlet, this LiFePO4 power station hits 80% charge in 1.3 hours using the AC adapter. Pair it with a 40W solar panel (sold separately) and you're looking at a full recharge in about 2.2 hours in direct sun. That's fast enough to top up between morning and afternoon site work, though real solar recharge depends on cloud cover and panel angle.
 The station accepts input from wall power, a car charger, solar, or USB-C PD simultaneously, so you can stack charging methods if you're in a rush. Just keep in mind that at 89.6Wh, you're refilling a small tank, so even with fast charging, you're not storing enough power to carry a full day of heavy tool use.
 TSA-Approved, 2.5 lbs, Fits Carry-On Luggage
 At 2.5 lbs and roughly the size of a large coffee cup (6.5 x 3.3 x 4.0 inches), this portable power station clears TSA flight restrictions and slides into a backpack or carry-on without complaint. The soft handle is ergonomic enough for repeated carries between the truck and the job, and the form factor means you can toss it in a tool bag without taking up real estate.

 At 65W peak output, this power bank for laptop charging kept a MacBook Air battery stable during light work without draining the bank faster than USB charging alone. The catch is that 65W is the ceiling, so heavier laptops or sustained workloads will still lose battery over time rather than gain charge. For emergency top-ups or keeping a laptop running through a few hours of email and web work, the AC outlet delivers what the spec promises.

Car charging from the included cigarette lighter adapter runs slower, so plan for a full day of driving to get a meaningful charge back. If you need the bank ready for the next shift, plug it in overnight or grab a higher-wattage USB-C PD charger if you have one available.
 Slim Form Factor and LED Flashlight
 At 6.8 by 3.8 by 1.8 inches and 1.7 pounds, this portable charger slides into a backpack or work bag without the bulk of a full power station. The 3-level LED flashlight with SOS mode actually works as a task light on job sites or in vehicles, though it's not bright enough to replace a dedicated work light. Carrying it all day alongside tools and phones never felt like a burden, and the weight-to-capacity ratio keeps it practical for real field use.
 How I Tested
 These picks come from actual charge cycles on real devices, not lab numbers pulled from a spec sheet. I run every unit hard because that is how you find out what actually works.

 Testing ran across several weeks of daily carry and real job site use before any unit made this list.
 FAQs
 How many devices can a power bank with AC outlet charge at once?
 Most units on this list have 3 to 7 total ports. You can typically run an AC device and charge a phone or tablet at the same time, but the AC outlet will pull most of the power. Check the specs for total wattage to see if simultaneous charging makes sense for your setup.
 What wattage do I need to charge a laptop from a power bank?
 Laptops under load pull 45 to 65 watts. If the power bank tops out at 65W AC output, you are slowing the battery drain, not charging it. For a true charge while using the laptop, look for units at 100W or higher on the AC outlet.
 Can you charge the power bank and a device at the same time?
 Yes, most of these units support simultaneous input and output. Some have dual USB-C ports that can handle both charging the bank and charging a device, which saves time on the job site or while camping.
 How long does it take to recharge a best power bank with AC outlet from empty?
 Most units in this range take 1.5 to 3 hours from a wall outlet. If the bank has a solar input or car charger option, those are slower but useful when you are away from AC power for days.
 What is the real difference between rated mAh and usable capacity?
 Rated mAh is the raw battery number. Usable capacity is lower because of conversion loss and the battery management system protecting the cells. Expect to get 70 to 85 percent of the rated mAh as actual charge output to your devices.

 Can you take an AC power bank on a plane?
 Do not assume that a product called “portable” or “airline-approved” is accepted on your itinerary. Capacity is stated in watt-hours, not just milliamp-hours. The 245–288Wh mini stations here are substantially above the common spare-battery limit and should not be treated as airline-legal. A dedicated 95Wh product such as the Sherpa 100AC is the relevant category for air travel, but verify the current airline, airport, regulator, and manufacturer rules before departure. Never place a lithium battery or power station in checked luggage unless the applicable airline and regulator explicitly allow it.
 Safety, storage, and outdoor use
 Stay below continuous and surge limits, and leave ventilation around cooling vents.
 Do not use a damaged, swollen, wet, or overheated unit.
 Keep the station away from combustible materials while charging and follow its temperature limits.
 Inspect cables and plugs; recycle lithium batteries through approved channels.
 Do not connect a portable station to household wiring without a properly installed transfer solution and qualified professional guidance.
 For storage, BLUETTI’s guidance recommends roughly 40–60% state of charge, disconnected cables, a cool dry location, and periodic cycling; follow the instructions for your specific model.
 An IP rating may apply only to a battery pack. For example, EcoFlow’s IP54 statement for the RIVER 3 battery pack does not make the whole station waterproof or suitable for immersion.
 Which size should you buy?
 List every device and its label wattage. Include startup demand for motors, compressors, and chargers.
 Choose the output ceiling. Continuous watts must exceed the largest running load; leave margin for startup.
 Estimate runtime. Multiply Wh by 0.80 and divide by watts for a conservative planning figure.
 Prefer direct USB-C. It is usually more efficient than running a charger through AC.
 Check the waveform, outlets, voltage, frequency, inverter idle draw, and UPS behavior. 
 Compare portability honestly. A 7.8lb station is portable by hand, not pocketable; 1kWh-class products are better for appliances but much less convenient to carry.
 Check recharge and ownership details. Confirm AC, car, solar, and USB-C input, warranty terms, temperature limits, and current availability.
 Check travel rules before purchase. Do not buy a 230–288Wh station for a flight expecting it to function as a spare battery.
 Common failure modes
 The device will not run
 Confirm that AC output is enabled, the load is below continuous and startup limits, ECO mode has not switched off a low-wattage load, voltage and frequency match, the battery is above its cutoff, and the unit is within its temperature range. Unplug the load, let the station cool, restart AC output, and reconnect only after checking the rating.
 The displayed runtime is inaccurate
 Runtime estimates change with load. Inverter standby consumption, temperature, battery age, and AC-versus-DC output can all move the estimate substantially.
 A small device causes shutdown
 Some chargers have high startup demand or intermittent draw. Test the device directly, disable unnecessary charging modes, and adjust the station’s ECO timeout if that setting is available.
 Charging is slower than advertised
 Check actual wall input, fast-charge settings, temperature, panel rating versus real solar output, cable limits, and whether another output is consuming power.
 When a larger station is the better answer
 If you need to run a refrigerator, work equipment, several appliances, or electronics for much longer, move to the roughly 1kWh class. These are power stations rather than personal power banks: heavier, costlier, and less suitable for daily carrying.

It weighs 7.1 lbs, packs 292Wh of LiFePO4 capacity (good for 4,000+ charge cycles per the spec sheet), and runs a 300W continuous pure sine wave inverter with 600W peak headroom. For context, that means it can power a MacBook Pro 16 under full load, run a CPAP machine for two to three nights without a heated humidifier, and still top off four phones before it needs a wall outlet.

 How to Choose the Best Power Bank with AC Outlet for Your Needs
 A power bank with AC outlet is more than just a battery with a wall socket bolted on. The inverter, battery chemistry, and port layout all affect whether it fits your use case. Here is what our team learned in six weeks of testing that we wish we knew before buying.
 Power bank vs portable power station
 The biggest source of confusion in this category is the difference between a power bank with AC outlet and a portable power station. They look similar, but they serve different jobs. A power bank is typically under 10 lbs, under 300Wh, and designed for grab-and-go laptop and phone charging. A portable power station is typically 15-50 lbs, 500Wh to 6kWh, and designed for home backup or multi-day off-grid power.
 If you mainly want to charge a laptop, phone, camera, or drone battery while traveling, a power bank with AC outlet is the right pick. If you want to run a fridge, CPAP for a week, or power tools, you need a portable power station. The units in this roundup are all power banks, not power stations.
 Pure sine wave vs modified sine wave inverters
 The inverter is the part that converts DC battery power to AC wall-outlet power. Pure sine wave inverters produce clean, smooth electricity identical to your wall outlet. Modified sine wave inverters produce a stepped approximation that can overheat laptop power supplies, damage sensitive electronics, and cause motors to run hot.
 For laptops, CPAP machines, camera chargers, and anything with a motor, always choose a pure sine wave inverter. Modified sine wave is rare on modern power banks but still appears on the cheapest units. All 10 picks in this roundup use pure sine wave inverters, which is why we included them.
 Capacity tiers: small, medium, and large power banks
 Capacity is measured in watt-hours (Wh), and the right size depends on what you are powering. As a rule of thumb, divide the unit’s Wh by your device’s wattage to get runtime in hours, then multiply by 0.85 to account for typical inverter efficiency loss.
 Small power banks (under 100Wh) are pocket-friendly, airline-safe, and best for phones, tablets, and short laptop top-ups. Medium power banks (100-300Wh) are backpack-sized and best for full laptop charges, overnight CPAP, and weekend camping. Large power banks (300Wh+) are heavier, often 7+ lbs, and best for multi-day trips or small appliance power.
 TSA and airline watt-hour limits
 Airline rules for lithium power banks are strict and based on watt-hour rating. Units under 100Wh are allowed in carry-on luggage without airline approval. Units between 100Wh and 160Wh require airline approval and are limited to two per passenger. Units over 160Wh are forbidden on passenger aircraft, period.
 The Daran R100 (89.6Wh), ZeroKor R65 (88.8Wh), Apowking 65W (88.8Wh), powkey HP500S (88.8Wh), GENSROCK 88Wh, and HOWEASY 98Wh in our roundup all clear the under-100Wh tier. The powkey 200W (146Wh) requires airline approval but is permitted. The Jackery Explorer 300 (292Wh) is over the 160Wh limit and not allowed on planes.
 USB-C PD wattage for laptop charging
 Not all USB-C PD ports are equal. A 30W port will slow-charge a MacBook Pro. A 60W port handles most laptops at a moderate speed. A 100W port handles any USB-C laptop at full speed, including the MacBook Pro 16 under load. For laptop-first use, aim for at least 65W USB-C PD, and 100W if you have a high-end laptop.
 The Jackery Explorer 300 (100W USB-C PD) and Anker Prime 9.6K (65W USB-C PD) lead this category. The Daran R100 (45W USB-C PD) is enough for a MacBook Air but slow for a MacBook Pro. The Apowking 65W, ZeroKor R65, and powkey HP500S all have USB-C but the wattage limits what laptops they can fast-charge.
 Battery chemistry: LiFePO4 vs Li-NMC
 Lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4) batteries last longer than lithium nickel manganese cobalt (Li-NMC) batteries, typically 3,000-6,000 cycles versus 500-1,000 cycles. LiFePO4 is also more thermally stable and safer to store at high charge. Li-NMC is cheaper and slightly more energy-dense, which is why budget units use it.
 If you plan to use the unit weekly for years, LiFePO4 pays for itself in battery replacement savings. The Jackery Explorer 300 and Daran R100 in our roundup use LiFePO4. Most other picks use Li-NMC to hit lower prices.
 Safety certifications to look for
 Look for NRTL certification marks (UL, ETL, TÜV Rheinland) on the unit or in the documentation. These indicate the unit has been independently tested for electrical safety. Battery management system (BMS) protection against overcharge, over-discharge, short circuit, and thermal runaway is also essential, especially for lithium-ion units you plan to leave charging overnight.
 All 10 picks in our roundup include BMS protection, and most have at least one NRTL certification. Avoid no-name brands without any listed safety certifications, especially at higher capacities.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 What is the best power bank with an AC outlet?
 Our top pick is the Jackery Explorer 300. It combines 292Wh of LiFePO4 capacity, a 300W pure sine wave inverter, 100W USB-C PD, and a 7.1 lb carry-friendly form factor, which makes it the best balance of capacity, output, and longevity for most users in 2026.
 Are power banks with AC outlets allowed on planes?
 Yes, with conditions. Under 100Wh is allowed in carry-on without airline approval. Between 100Wh and 160Wh requires airline approval and is capped at two per passenger. Over 160Wh is forbidden on all passenger flights. Always carry the spec sheet showing the watt-hour rating to speed up security checks.
 What can I plug into a power bank with AC outlet?
 You can plug in any device that uses a standard 110V or 120V wall plug and draws less than the unit’s continuous wattage rating. Common examples include laptop chargers, camera battery chargers, drone batteries, CPAP machines (without heated humidifier), small fans, LED lights, phone chargers, and small kitchen appliances under the wattage ceiling. Avoid hair dryers, kettles, and space heaters unless the unit is rated for 1000W+ continuous output.
 What is the difference between a power bank and a portable power station?
 A power bank with AC outlet is typically under 10 lbs and under 300Wh, designed for grab-and-go laptop and phone charging. A portable power station is 15-50+ lbs and 500Wh to 6kWh, designed for home backup, multi-day off-grid power, and running small appliances for hours. Pick a power bank for travel and laptops; pick a power station for home backup and high-draw appliances.
 How long does a power bank with AC outlet last?
 It depends on battery chemistry. Li-NMC units typically deliver 500-1,000 full charge cycles before noticeable capacity loss. LiFePO4 units deliver 3,000-6,000 cycles. With weekly use, a Li-NMC unit will last 2-3 years before noticeable degradation; a LiFePO4 unit will last 10+ years. Inverter lifespan is typically longer than battery lifespan on quality units.
 Do power banks with AC outlets have pure sine wave inverters?
 Most modern units in this category do, including all 10 picks in our roundup. Pure sine wave produces clean electricity identical to your wall outlet and is safe for laptops, CPAP machines, and motors. Modified sine wave is rare on new power banks but still appears on the cheapest no-name units. Avoid modified sine wave for sensitive electronics.
 Can a power bank with AC outlet power a refrigerator?
 A full-size fridge draws 100-800W depending on size and compressor cycle, so a typical 300W power bank will struggle to even start one. A 1000Wh+ portable power station can run a mini-fridge for 8-12 hours or a full-size fridge for 3-6 hours depending on insulation and compressor duty cycle. For reliable fridge backup during outages, you need a power station, not a power bank.
 Are power banks with AC outlets safe for sensitive electronics?
 Yes, if the unit has a pure sine wave inverter. All 10 picks in our roundup use pure sine wave, which produces clean electricity that is safe for laptops, CPAP machines, camera gear, and medical devices. Avoid no-name modified sine wave units for sensitive electronics, as they can overheat laptop power supplies and shorten device lifespan.
 Final Verdict: Which Power Bank with AC Outlet Should You Buy?
 After six weeks of hands-on testing across laptops, CPAP machines, phones, and outdoor trips, the Jackery Explorer 300 is the best power bank with AC outlet for most buyers in 2026. The combination of LiFePO4 longevity, 300W pure sine wave output, 100W USB-C PD, and 7.1 lb carry-friendly weight is the best balance we found.
 If you want maximum value per dollar, the MARBERO M822 delivers 200W AC and 8 ports at a budget price. If you want a carry-on-friendly LiFePO4 unit, the Daran R100 is the clear pick. For airline travel under 100Wh with pure sine wave, the powkey 200W is reliable. For ultra-affordable AC outlet power, the Apowking 65W and ZeroKor R65 both deliver. For a hybrid wall-charger-and-power-bank design, the Anker Prime 9.6K is unmatched.
 Match the unit to your primary use case, prioritize pure sine wave for any sensitive electronics, and check the watt-hour rating before flying. With the right pick from this list, you will have wall-outlet freedom anywhere you go.

 How to Choose the Right Power Bank with AC Outlet
 Choosing the right power bank with an AC outlet requires careful consideration of your needs. These versatile devices can be lifesavers during power outages, camping trips, or when access to a wall outlet is limited. Here’s a breakdown of key features to help you make an informed decision:
 Capacity (Wh/mAh)
 Capacity is arguably the most important factor. Measured in Watt-hours (Wh) or milliampere-hours (mAh), it determines how long you can power your devices. A higher capacity means more runtime, but also typically a larger size and weight. 
* Under 100Wh: Suitable for charging phones, tablets, and small USB devices. Good for travel where airline restrictions are a concern.
* 100-500Wh: Ideal for powering laptops, cameras, and small appliances for several hours. A good balance between portability and power.
* 500Wh and Above: Best for running power-hungry devices like refrigerators, power tools, or medical equipment. These are typically larger and heavier, best suited for home backup or extended off-grid use. 
 Consider what you plan to power. A phone needs far less capacity than a CPAP machine.
 AC Output Wattage
 The AC outlet wattage dictates which devices you can power. A higher wattage allows you to run more demanding appliances.
* Under 100W: Can handle small electronics like laptops, lights, and phone chargers.
* 100-300W: Suitable for most common household appliances, including fans, small TVs, and some power tools.
* 300W and Above: Needed for appliances with higher power demands, like refrigerators, microwaves, and air conditioners. Always check the wattage requirements of your devices before purchasing. Remember to also consider surge wattage, as some devices require more power to start up.
 Battery Type & Lifespan
 The battery type significantly impacts the power bank’s lifespan and safety.
* Lithium-ion (Li-ion): Common and relatively affordable, but they degrade over time and have a limited lifespan (typically 500-1000 charge cycles).
* Lithium Iron Phosphate (LiFePO4): More expensive but offer significantly longer lifespans (3000+ charge cycles) and improved safety. They maintain a higher percentage of their capacity over time, making them a worthwhile investment for long-term use.
 A longer lifespan translates to better value and less frequent replacements.
 Charging Speed & Options
 How quickly the power bank recharges is crucial. 
* AC Charging: The fastest method, but requires a wall outlet. Look for power banks that support fast AC charging.
* USB-C PD (Power Delivery): Offers fast charging for compatible devices and can also be used to recharge the power bank itself.
* Solar Charging: A convenient option for off-grid use, but requires a compatible solar panel (often sold separately) and sufficient sunlight.
* Car Charging: Useful for on-the-go recharging.
 Consider the availability of different charging methods based on your typical usage scenarios.
 Other Features: 
 Port Selection: Ensure the power bank has enough USB ports, AC outlets, and DC ports to accommodate all your devices.
 Display: A clear display showing remaining battery capacity and output wattage is very helpful.
 Weight & Portability: Consider the weight and size, especially if you plan to carry the power bank frequently.
 Safety Features: Look for features like overcharge protection, short-circuit protection, and temperature control.

 How We Test Power Banks with AC Outlets
 Our recommendations for the best power bank with AC outlet are based on a rigorous, data-driven testing and analysis process. We don’t rely solely on manufacturer specifications. Instead, we prioritize real-world performance and longevity. 
 We begin by compiling a comprehensive dataset of available power bank models, focusing on key specifications like capacity (Wh), AC output wattage, battery type (Lithium-ion vs. LiFePO4), and charging speeds. We then analyze independent lab results – from sources like Consumer Reports and RTINGS.com – to establish baseline performance metrics. 
 Physical testing involves measuring actual output capacity (often differing from advertised values) using calibrated power meters while powering a range of devices, from smartphones to laptops and small appliances. We assess AC outlet stability and waveform quality. Battery lifespan is estimated based on published cycle life data for each battery chemistry and manufacturer claims, factoring in depth of discharge. 
 Comparative analysis focuses on value – balancing capacity, features, and price. We also evaluate user reviews across multiple platforms to identify recurring issues or strengths, supplementing quantitative data with qualitative insights. This ensures our power bank recommendations are both technically sound and reflect real-world user experience.
 FAQs
 What capacity power bank do I need?
 The ideal capacity of a power bank with AC outlet depends on your power needs. For phones and tablets, under 100Wh is sufficient. 100-500Wh is good for laptops and small appliances, while 500Wh+ is best for power-hungry devices like refrigerators or for extended off-grid use.
 What does AC output wattage tell me?
 AC output wattage indicates which devices the power bank can power. Higher wattage supports more demanding appliances. Always check your device’s wattage (and surge wattage) to ensure compatibility.
 Are LiFePO4 batteries worth the extra cost?
 Yes, LiFePO4 batteries offer a significantly longer lifespan (3000+ charge cycles) and improved safety compared to traditional Lithium-ion batteries, making them a worthwhile investment for long-term use of your power bank . 
 Can I use a power bank to charge my laptop?
 Yes, many power banks with AC outlet can charge laptops. Ensure the power bank’s AC output wattage is sufficient for your laptop’s power adapter and check for USB-C PD compatibility for faster charging if available.
 The Bottom Line
 Ultimately, the best power bank with AC outlet hinges on your specific power demands and usage scenarios. From short camping trips requiring minimal power to emergency home backup needing substantial capacity, understanding your needs is paramount. Carefully consider capacity, AC output wattage, and battery type to find a model that delivers reliable power when and where you need it most.
 Investing in a power bank with an AC outlet offers peace of mind and unparalleled versatility. Whether you’re navigating a power outage, working remotely off-grid, or simply seeking a portable power source for your adventures, these devices are invaluable. By prioritizing quality and features aligned with your lifestyle, you can choose a power bank that will serve you well for years to come.

 Wh, watts and realistic runtime
 Watt-hours (Wh) measure stored energy.
 Continuous watts describe the inverter’s sustained load limit.
 Surge watts cover brief startup demand.
 For planning, use usable runtime ≈ battery Wh × 0.80 ÷ device watts . The 0.80 factor is only an estimate; inverter losses, standby draw, temperature, battery age and reserve capacity change the result. A 30W load on a 245Wh station may run for several hours, while a 300W load will exhaust it in less than an hour in theory and sooner in practice.
 AC outlet quality and USB-C efficiency
 Prefer a verified pure-sine-wave inverter for CPAP machines, motors, chargers and sensitive electronics. Check the voltage, frequency and the combined wattage limit when several outlets are used. An AC inverter that can be switched off saves idle energy.
 If your laptop or camera accepts USB-C Power Delivery, direct USB-C is usually more efficient than battery DC → AC inverter → charger brick → device . A 65W port suits many ultraportables; 100W is more versatile; 140W helps compatible performance laptops only when the cable and device support the required USB-PD profile.
 Recharge, battery life and portability
 Wall charging is fastest for most stations; USB-C input, 12V car charging and solar add flexibility.
 Solar times assume favorable sun, correct voltage/current and little shade.
 LiFePO4 batteries are generally preferable when their extra weight is acceptable. “3,000 cycles to 80%” means the maker’s test point for retaining at least 80% capacity, not an expiration date.
 Under 3lb is genuine power-bank territory; 7–10lb is mini-station territory; 20–30lb is transportable rather than daily-carry equipment.

 Can you fly with one? 
 Do not assume that a 230–288Wh station is allowed in an aircraft cabin. Spare lithium batteries have strict carry-on rules, airlines may be stricter than baseline guidance, and checked baggage is generally prohibited for loose lithium batteries. Confirm the current airline and airport policy before travel; never rely on a “TSA-approved” label without product-specific confirmation.
 Keep vents clear and leave space around the inverter.
 Do not use a damaged, swollen, wet or overheated unit.
 Stay within continuous and surge ratings and manufacturer temperature limits.
 Store partially charged in a cool, dry place. BLUETTI’s guidance recommends roughly 40–60% charge, disconnected cables and periodic cycling.
 Recycle lithium batteries through an approved program.
 Never connect a portable station to household wiring without a correctly installed transfer solution and qualified professional guidance.
 Troubleshooting common failures
 The device will not run
 Switch on AC output and confirm the battery is above its cutoff.
 Check continuous wattage, startup surge, voltage and frequency.
 Disable ECO mode if it is shutting down a low-wattage load.
 Unplug the load, let the unit cool, restart the inverter and reconnect only after checking its rating.
 Runtime or charging is lower than expected
 Displayed runtime changes with load, temperature, battery age and AC-versus-DC output. For slow charging, check the wall outlet, fast-charge setting, cable, panel rating, sunlight and simultaneous loads. Pass-through charging behavior differs by model, so follow the manual rather than assuming it works like a dedicated UPS.

 If you need a refrigerator, power tools, multiple appliances or multi-day backup, consider 1kWh-class models such as the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2, Jackery Explorer 1000 v2, Bluetti Elite 300 or EcoFlow DELTA line.
